analysis.one_liner: Guarantees workers paid vacation: one hour earned per 25 hours worked, up to two weeks a year.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let workers earn up to 80 hours of paid vacation a year, was referred to the Senate labor committee in August 2026 and has had no hearing, vote, or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires nearly every employer — from a one-person shop to a big corporation to state and local governments — to let workers earn one hour of paid leave for every 25 hours worked, capped at 80 hours (about two weeks for a full-time worker) a year. Workers could use the time for any reason, keep health and other benefits while out, carry over up to 40 unused hours, and get cash for unused time if they leave the job. The bill bars employers from retaliating against workers who use the leave and lets workers sue or file a complaint with the Labor Department if they're denied it.
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest winners are workers who currently get little or no paid vacation — most often part-time, hourly, and low-wage employees in retail, restaurants, and care work. The United States is the only advanced economy with no national paid-vacation guarantee, and no federal law requires any vacation at all, so this would create a floor for everyone from fast-food cashiers to federal employees. Tipped workers would be paid at least the full minimum wage rate while on leave, part-time workers accrue at the same rate as full-timers, and employers cannot demand to know why someone is taking the time or make them find their own replacement first.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Part-time and low-wage workers without paid vacation

how_it_helps.text: Every covered worker — including part-time and tipped employees — begins earning paid leave from their first day on the job, at a rate of one hour for every 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours in a 12-month period.
Leave can be used for any reason, in one-hour increments, without telling the employer why, and employers cannot make workers find a replacement as a condition of taking time off.
Workers keep their benefits (including health insurance) while on leave, can carry over up to 40 unused hours to the next year, and must be paid out for unused earned leave if they are fired or quit.

The bill makes retaliation illegal — firing, cutting shifts, or counting leave use under a no-fault attendance policy — and gives workers a private right to sue for lost wages, interest, and liquidated damages, with attorney's fees paid by a losing employer; the Labor Department can also investigate and sue.
The bill does not override stronger state or local paid-leave laws, union contracts, or employer policies that already offer more time.

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay — essentially any business with at least one employee operating 20 or more weeks a year, plus nonprofits, public agencies, and state and local governments. The cost is roughly two weeks of wages per full-time employee per year, plus recordkeeping and scheduling administration (the bill requires notice postings, a written leave policy, and a system showing each worker their accrued balance). Businesses would absorb that through margins, prices, or slower hiring, and governments through budgets. Existing collective bargaining agreements get up to 18 months before the requirement applies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers of all sizes, including small businesses and governments

drawbacks.text: The cost falls hardest on small and low-margin employers, since coverage starts at just one employee; a shop with a handful of workers would owe roughly two weeks of pay per person per year, which could mean slower hiring, fewer hours, or higher prices.

The mandate is blunt about scheduling: employers may reject a requested date only for a 'bona fide business reason,' must offer an alternative within 30 days, and cannot require workers to find their own coverage — which could strain staffing at small restaurants, clinics, and seasonal businesses.
The 80-hour annual cap and 40-hour carryover limit mean a two-week maximum; the bill creates a floor but would not require employers with stingier policies to offer substantially more time.

The state-employee provision is aggressive: any state taking federal money for a program effectively waives its constitutional immunity to employee lawsuits over the leave, which several states would challenge in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and broad: tens of millions of American workers, disproportionately low-wage and part-time, get a guaranteed paid break that federal law currently does not require at all, with teeth (payout, anti-retaliation, private lawsuits) that make it more than a suggestion. The cost is genuine but diffused — it lands on employers of every size rather than one industry, and it is essentially a wage in kind rather than a new tax. The design is careful about the main practical objection (chaotic scheduling) by allowing limited business-reason restrictions and waiving notice in emergencies. The honest tradeoff is that some small businesses and governments will feel the payroll cost, and the most aggressive provision — conditioning states' immunity on federal funds — invites litigation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate in August 2026 and sent to the committee that handles labor bills, where it has sat with no hearing, committee vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Guaranteed Paid Vacation Act on August 6, 2026, joined by four Democratic senators — Murphy, Markey, Gallego, and Padilla.

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, the panel that would normally write and vote on labor legislation before anything reaches the floor.
No further action appears in the record: the committee has not held a hearing or markup, and the full Senate has not voted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers that do not pay vacation are better off: nothing has changed for them, while workers without paid leave are no closer to getting it. The outcome is not final — the Senate's term runs to January 3, 2027 — but a bill with no movement five months in has the usual profile of one that will not be revived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers with no paid-vacation obligation, for now

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and has pushed versions of a federal paid-vacation guarantee in earlier Congresses.

for.name: Chris Murphy, Ed Markey, Ruben Gallego, and Alex Padilla
for.role: U.S. Senators (D-CT, D-MA, D-AZ, D-CA), original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only four cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and has held no hearing or markup on it; without committee action a bill cannot reach the Senate floor.

against.name: Business and employer lobbies (e.g., the U.S. Chamber of Commerce)
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed federal paid-leave mandates as costly to employers; no specific opposition to this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats or Senator Sanders, an Independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor has signed on — against a Senate run by Republicans, the bill's support is entirely one-sided.

industries.note: These industries employ the largest share of the part-time, hourly, and tipped workers who currently get little or no paid vacation, so the cost of the mandate — roughly two weeks of pay per worker per year — falls on them most heavily. The bill also prohibits the common practices (no-fault attendance penalties, requiring workers to find coverage) these employers use to discourage leave-taking.

Coverage starts at a single employee, so the smallest shops bear per-worker costs similar to large firms while having the least ability to absorb scheduling gaps or build payroll software systems to track accrued leave.

Public agencies count as employers under the bill, and any state accepting federal funds for a program waives its immunity to employee suits under it — a direct budget and litigation exposure for state and local payrolls.

industries.industry: Large employers with existing generous vacation policies
industries.note: Firms that already offer two weeks or more and have higher leave standards are largely unaffected, because the bill is a floor that yields to stronger employer policies, union contracts, and state laws — they gain a level playing field against competitors that offer nothing.

analysis.trajectory: The Senate remains in session until January 3, 2027, but the bill's path is close to closed: it has sat in the HELP Committee for months with no hearing or markup scheduled, in a committee chaired by the opposition party, with no Republican cosponsors. Sanders has introduced this same paid-vacation guarantee in previous Congresses and it has never advanced to a committee vote or floor action. Barring an attachment to a larger package, it will almost certainly die when this Congress ends, and its realistic future is reintroduction in the next one.
